objectives: Propose features and data sources, and name the leakage each could bring.

screens.title: Four features, one label
screens.prose: About ten minutes with the code. Write `feature_corrs(path)`. It builds four features and correlates each with tomorrow's log return, on the rows where all exist.
screens.question: Write `feature_corrs(path)`.

widget.starter:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def feature_corrs(path):
    """Correlation of four features with y, the next log return.
    Keys: 'ret', 'mean5', 'logvol', 'centred3'.
    mean5 ends today; centred3 is centred on today.
    Use only rows where y and every feature exist."""
    df = pd.read_csv(path)
    # Your code here
    return {}
widget.solution:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def feature_corrs(path):
    df = pd.read_csv(path)
    df['ret'] = np.log(df['close']).diff()
    df['y'] = df['ret'].shift(-1)
    df['mean5'] = df['ret'].rolling(5).mean()
    df['centred3'] = df['ret'].rolling(3, center=True).mean()
    df['logvol'] = np.log(df['volume'])
    d = df.dropna(subset=['y', 'ret', 'mean5', 'centred3'])
    return {c: float(d[c].corr(d['y'])) for c in ['ret', 'mean5', 'logvol', 'centred3']}
widget.how: Check runs 5 hidden tests. Four check each correlation on the futures file (within 1e-6). One checks all four on a twelve-row file (relative 1e-9). Every correlation uses the same rows.

hints.text: Build `y` with `shift(-1)` on the log return.
`rolling(3, center=True)` looks one day ahead. Drop rows missing any of `y`, `ret`, `mean5`, `centred3`.
Then `d[c].corr(d['y'])` for each feature.

feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Use log returns, one shared set of rows, and `center=True` for the centred mean.

explain.text: Today's return correlates 0.126 with tomorrow's, the five-day mean 0.029 and log volume 0.030. The centred mean reaches 0.609 because it contains the label.

screens.title: Where a leak hides
screens.prose: Your model decides at the close for tomorrow's return. A data vendor supplies the fields. Some arrive later than they claim.
screens.question: Select all that apply. Which can leak the future?

options.text: Earnings restated months later, kept under the original date
Today's index members applied to every past year
A second asset's close stamped hours after your decision
A volume figure the vendor fills in the next evening
Yesterday's volume figure, read at today's close for tomorrow's label
options.why: It is known before the decision, so it is safe.

options.text: Today's close price, read at today's close for a next-day label
options.why: It is known at the decision time. The label is tomorrow's return.

hints.text: For each field, ask when it really became known.
Restated, back-filled and late-stamped fields carry later knowledge.
Four of the six arrive after the decision or use later facts.

feedback.correct: Restated figures, today's members, late stamps and next-evening fills all leak.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Check each field against the time you decide.

byKey.yvol: Yesterday's volume is known at the decision, so it does not leak.
byKey.today: Today's close is known at the decision, so it does not leak.

explain.text: Restatement, survivorship, late timestamps and back-filled fields are the usual routes. Each one hands the model something that was not yet known on the day.

It is the best feature, so I would build the whole model on it
options.why: You ranked features by correlation. A leaking feature scores well and cannot be used.

Days $t-1$, $t$ and $t+1$: one of them is the label.

byKey.neighbour: You read a pattern into it. The label is inside the average.

screens.title: Statistics from the future
screens.prose: A feature is a value minus its mean. The five values are 2, 4, 6, 8 and 20. On day 3 the value is 6. The line shows the mean of all five.
screens.question: What is the day-3 value minus the mean of the days known by day 3?

hints.text: Days 1 to 3 are the only days known on day 3.
Their mean is $(2 + 4 + 6)/3$.
The mean is 4, so $6 - 4 = 2$.

feedback.correct: 2. Use the mean of what you knew.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Average only days 1 to 3, then subtract.

byKey.full: You subtracted the full-sample mean of 8. That mean includes the jump on day 5.
byKey.raw: You did not subtract a mean at all.

explain.text: The full-sample mean of 8 contains the jump on day 5. On day 3 you only knew 2, 4 and 6, so the honest mean is 4.

screens.title: Say it aloud
screens.prose: A feature leaks when $t_{\text{known}} > t_{\text{decide}}$: it was known after the moment you decide. For a next-day label, $t_{\text{decide}}$ is the close of day $t$. Say that test in one sentence.
screens.question: Which sentence would you say?

options.text: For each feature I note when it is known: after my decision means a leak.
I drop any feature whose correlation with the label looks very high.
options.why: You tested the symptom. A leak can be small, and an honest feature can correlate well.

options.text: I avoid rolling windows, since they look at other days of data.
options.why: A window that ends at the decision time is safe. The end of the window is what matters.

options.text: I fit only on the training period, so nothing can leak at all.
options.why: That is the split. A feature can still use later data inside the training rows.

hints.text: Look for a test that names two times.
Leaks are about when something is known.
Only one option compares the time known with the time decided.

feedback.correct: Known time against decision time, feature by feature.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Pick the sentence that names two times.

byKey.corr: You used correlation. It is a symptom, not the test.
byKey.roll: You banned a safe tool. Window ends matter.
byKey.split: You described the split, not the feature.

explain.text: Write the time each feature becomes known and the time you decide. Anything known later is a leak, however well it scores.

screens.title: Why 0.577
screens.prose: Daily returns are independent with variance $\sigma^2$. The label is $y = r_{t+1}$. A feature is the centred mean $m = (r_t + r_{t+1} + r_{t+2})/3$.
screens.question: Put the lines in order. Leave out the step that does not belong.

lines.text: Three independent terms divided by 3 give $\text{Var}(m) = 3\sigma^2/9 = \sigma^2/3$.
The correlation is $\text{Cov}(m, y)$ over $\sqrt{\text{Var}(m)\,\text{Var}(y)}$, which is $\dfrac{\sigma^2/3}{\sqrt{\sigma^2/3}\,\sigma}$.
One term in three is the label, so the correlation is $1/3$.
lines.why: That is the covariance share. Dividing by both spreads gives $1/\sqrt{3}$.

hints.text: Start with what $m$ and $y$ share.
Covariance counts the shared term; variance counts all three.
Divide the covariance by both spreads.

feedback.correct: 0.5774, close to the 0.6086 in the file.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Covariance, variance, then the ratio.

byKey.x: You gave the share of the label inside the mean. A correlation divides by both spreads.
byKey.left-out: You left out a step the derivation needs.

explain.text: The mean of $w$ independent returns, one of them the label, correlates $1/\sqrt{w}$ with it. The file gives 0.609 against 0.577 for pure noise.

screens.prose: You decide at 16:35 for tomorrow's return. A vendor offers four daily fields. One is safe.
screens.question: Which field can feed the model?

options.text: The official close, published at 16:31
A consensus forecast revised at 20:00 and stamped 16:00
options.why: It is stamped before it was known. At 16:35 you cannot have it.

options.text: The volume-weighted price of the day, delivered at 18:00
The index membership list as it stands today

hints.text: Compare each time stamp with 16:35.
A safe field is published before the decision.
Only the official close is out by 16:31.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Check publication time against 16:35.

byKey.consensus: You trusted the stamp. The revision came at 20:00.
byKey.vwap: You used a field that arrives at 18:00.

explain.text: Judge a field by when it was actually available, not by the date printed on it. Vendors stamp the day a value refers to, not the day it arrived.

screens.title: The follow-up
screens.prose: The interviewer asks: "How would you check there is no leak?" Put your steps in order. Leave out the one you would not use.
screens.question: Order the checks.

lines.text: List when each feature becomes known and when the label is set.
Shift or drop any feature known after the decision time.
Score on a later period never used, and watch for a collapse.
Shuffle the label and score on a later period: a score clearly above chance means the pipeline leaks.
Keep any feature whose backtest correlation is high.
lines.why: High correlation is where leaks hide. It is not a check.

hints.text: Audit first, then fix, then test.
A leak shows as a score that collapses later.
List, shift, score later, shuffle.

feedback.correct: List, shift, score later, shuffle the label.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Audit the times, fix them, then test.

byKey.x: You kept the features that look best. Leaks look best.
byKey.left-out: You left out one of the four checks.

explain.text: The audit is a list of times. The tests are a later period and a shuffled label: a leak survives neither.

ideas: For every feature, write when it is known and when you decide. Known later means a leak.
A feature that contains the label correlates well and cannot be used: correlation is a symptom, not a test.
Rolling windows are safe when they end at the decision time, which `shift(1)` enforces.

formula.name: The leak test
formula.note: A mean of $w$ independent returns that contains the label correlates $1/\sqrt{w}$ with it.

summary.trap: A high correlation with the label is not a sign of a good feature.
